Muckraking. A form of investigative journalism emerged during the American Progressive Era, exposing corporate malfeasance, political corruption, and unsafe labor conditions through mass-circulation magazines and newspapers. Muckrakers used exposés, research, and vivid storytelling to shame industrial titans and politicians into reform. Their work catalyzed major legislation and fundamentally changed journalism's role as a public accountability tool. The term itself came from a character in John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress who could only see filth; President Theodore Roosevelt used it both supportively and dismissively as a nickname for the practice. Muckrakers published in journals of mass circulation like McClure's Magazine and Collier's, reaching millions of Americans previously insulated from knowledge of industrial exploitation. Upton Sinclair's The Jungle exposed rotting conditions in meatpacking plants. Ida B. Wells documented lynching and racial terror. Ida Tarbell revealed Standard Oil's predatory monopoly practices. These investigations forced legislative response. Food safety acts, trust-busting antitrust suits, labor laws, and campaign finance reforms emerged from pressure created by muckraking exposés. The practice declined after 1912 as magazines faced advertiser pressure, editorial constraints, and reader fatigue, having achieved its foundational goal of establishing accountability journalism. Muckraking distinguished itself from yellow journalism by its focus on documented fact and systemic reform rather than sensation for profit. Major muckraking publications included Arena, Everybody's Magazine, and The American, whose editors actively commissioned investigative series and backed their journalists against libel threats. These publications pioneered the modern journalistic technique of the multi-part series, investigations that could command reader attention over weeks and build pressure for legislative action incrementally.
